newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels seize key gateway towns to capital.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels seize key gateway towns to capital.

text.p: Rebel forces in Zaire announced the capture of three gateway towns to Kinshasa and military analysts said guerrillas were now in a position to choke off much of the capital's essential supplies.
"The rebel plan is becoming clearer now. They want to force the capital into submission, and the noose is tightening," said an analyst in Kinshasa.
A senior rebel official announced on Wednesday that Laurent Kabila's guerrillas had seized Ilebo, Tshikapa and Dowete.

Rebel "justice minister" Mwenge Kongolo said he believed the fall of Kinshasa was a "matter of days rather than weeks" and added that in his personal opinion there would not be a bloody battle for the capital.

A military official in Kinshasa said it was possible rebels had taken Ilebo and Tshikapa. "There were never any government troops in Ilebo and, at Tshikapa there were only a few gendarmes," said the officer, who asked not to be named.

Tshikapa, a diamond trading centre close to the Angolan border, is on the highway to the town of Kikwit, which shot into world limelight in mid-1995 because of an epidemic of the Ebola virus which killed more than 120 people there.

It is the most important town in Bandundu province, which supplies Kinshasa with most of its home produced food. Bandundu people are the majority in Kinshasa's population of more than five million and rebel incursions there will have a strong psychological impact on the capital, military analysts said.

The senior army officer was not sure about the capture of Dowete, a major town in President Mobutu Sese Seko's Equateur home province. It commands direct road access to Bandaka, a Zaire river port controlling important traffic to Kinshasa.

Ilebo is Zaire's largest inland port and second most important after its only sea port at Matadi on the country's small Atlantic coastline. It is the most vital link for goods destined for Kinshasa, transported by train from Lubumbashi and even South Africa, then transhipped by river to the capital.

While military analysts doubt Kabila will expose his men by sending them down the river to Kinshasa, they say rebels can effectively use the rail to bring massive reinforcements to Ilebo to try and cut off Kinshasa.
Life in Kinshasa appeared normal on Thursday after the rebel announcements and diplomats said this reflected the growing feeling that rebels will probably take the capital without serious resistance.
"It is apparent that the leaders of this country will not opt for the suicidal path of a bloody confrontation," one Western diplomat said.

Publicly, emergency rule prime minister General Likulia Bolongo vowed this week that government troops would defend Kinshasa to the last man. But throughout the six-month-old civil war, the same army has fled at the slightest sign of rebels, who have gone on to seize more than half the country, which is the size of Western Europe.
The United States meanwhile warned the rebels that they could be damaging future relations with Western powers by failing to repatriate Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire.
Washington said on Wednesday reports of mass killings of refugees were "of grave concern".
The rebels said they might allow aid workers on Thursday to reach two camps south of Kisangani where villagers reported fierce fighting between refugees and rebel forces.

The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR and some journalists were told by rebel authorities to be on standby for a visit to the camps, sealed off since Monday. UNHCR fears many of the 80,000 refugees south of Kisangani have already fled the fighting.
The rebels' apparent decision to allow access to the camps came after U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he was "shocked and appalled by the inhumanity" of their action.
Zairean villagers said on Wednesday Tutsi-dominated rebels had killed many Rwandan Hutu refugees at Kasese, just south of Kisangani, where 55,000 were in makeshift camps.
Most of the refugees are Rwandan Hutus who fled their country after the 1994 massacre of hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Tutsis and moderate Hutus by Hutu troops and militia.
Ethnic Tutsis launched Zaire's civil war in October and are still the spearhead of Kabila's rebels.
Efforts to end the six-month-old conflict peacefully are deadlocked over the venue of proposed direct talks between Kabila and the embattled Mobutu.
